name: Paraguay
summary: A landlocked South American country, independent since 1811, devastated by the War of the Triple Alliance (1864–70) and notable for its widespread Guaraní language.

knownFor.label: Itaipu Dam
knownFor.note: One of the world’s largest hydroelectric dams, shared with Brazil.

location.value: South America, landlocked; 406,752 km² (infobox), 406,796 km² in the department table.

terrain.value: Fertile east; the dry Chaco in the west.

climate.value: Subtropical: hot, humid summers and mild winters in the east; hotter and drier in the Chaco to the west.

resources.value: Fertile farmland for soybeans and cattle, and huge hydropower from the Itaipú (with Brazil) and Yacyretá (with Argentina) dams.

disasters.value: Floods along the Paraguay River, droughts that lower river levels and hurt shipping, and forest fires in the Chaco.

urbanisation.value: About two-thirds urban; the capital Asunción and its metropolitan area, plus Ciudad del Este and Encarnación.

disease.value: Dengue outbreaks are common; the World Health Organization certified Paraguay free of malaria in 2018.

migration.value: Mennonite and other immigrants settled the Chaco.

economicBase.value: The sixth-largest soybean producer and ninth-largest beef exporter; the page calls it the world’s largest exporter of electric power (2016 data), with the Itaipú dam among the largest hydroelectric stations.

tradeRoutes.value: Barges down the Paraguay and Paraná rivers to the Río de la Plata and the Atlantic; roads and the Friendship Bridge to Brazil.

moneyAndTax.value: The guaraní, the national currency since 1943, named after the Guaraní people.

inequality.value: Land is very unequally owned, with large ranches and soy farms beside many small farmers and landless peasants.

governmentType.value: A unitary presidential republic; Alfredo Stroessner ruled from a coup on 4 May 1954 until his overthrow on 3 February 1989 (a “35-year regime”).

succession.value: Since the fall of Stroessner (1989), presidents have been chosen in elections; the 1992 constitution limits them to one five-year term.

institutions.value: The 1992 constitution set up an elected president, a two-chamber Congress (Senate and Chamber of Deputies) and a Supreme Court of Justice.

stability.value: Long dictatorships under Francia (1814–40) and Stroessner (1954–89), with frequent coups and revolts between them.

eliteConflict.value: Rivalry between the Colorado Party, in power for most of the time since the late 1940s, and the Liberal Party.

armyAndTech.value: Small armed forces today; in the 1860s Paraguay had one of South America’s largest armies, and it fought the Chaco War in the 1930s.

majorWars.value: Triple Alliance War (1864–1870): at least half of Paraguayans died and 25–33% of its territory was lost; Chaco War with Bolivia (1932–35).
majorWars.source: Wikipedia: Paraguay (checked 13 Nov 2026); Britannica: history of Paraguay (checked 15 Nov 2026) (Britannica says more than half of Paraguay’s former population died in the 1864–70 war and gives no territory percentage; the Chaco War cease-fire was on 12 June 1935 and the 1938 treaty gave Paraguay three-fourths of the Chaco)

territoryChange.value: Lost land in 1870; gained the Chaco in 1935.

alliancesRivals.value: A founding member of Mercosur (1991) with Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay; old rivalries with Bolivia and its larger neighbours.

inventions.value: Few major inventions; the sweet leaf stevia (ka’a he’ẽ), long used by the Guaraní, was described by science from Paraguay.

scienceEducation.value: Adult literacy is over 90%; the National University of Asunción, the oldest university, was founded in 1889.

openness.value: Closed under Francia (1814–40), who restricted trade and travel; more open under the López family, and a trading nation today.

communicationTransport.value: River transport on the Paraná and Paraguay.

languageWriting.value: Spanish and Guaraní are both official (since 1992); most people speak Guaraní, many as their first language.

artsArchitecture.value: Ñandutí (spider-web) lace from Itauguá, harp and guarania music, and the ruins of Jesuit missions such as Trinidad.

sharedIdentity.value: The Guaraní language, memories of the War of the Triple Alliance and the Chaco War, and pride in independence.

dailyLife.value: Houses with patios; chipa, sopa paraguaya, tereré.

neighbours.value: Brazil to the east, Argentina to the south and west, and Bolivia to the north-west.

ideasReligions.value: The Jesuit missions (1600s–1767) shaped Guaraní Catholicism; nationalist memories of Francia and the López family remain strong.

colonisation.value: Part of the Spanish Empire from the founding of Asunción (1537) until independence in May 1811.

riseSignals.value: Juan de Salazar de Espinosa founded Asunción on 15 August 1537.
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Paraguay (checked 13 Nov 2026); Britannica: history of Paraguay (checked 15 Nov 2026) (Britannica says the first settlements date from 1536–56 under Domingo Martínez de Irala and does not give 15 August 1537)

peakPeriod.value: The 2000s–2010s brought fast growth from soy, beef and hydropower; some see the 1850s under Carlos Antonio López as an earlier high point.

declineSignals.value: War losses (1864–70) killed a large share of the population.

outcome.value: Paraguay overthrew the Spanish administration on 14 May 1811.
outcome.source: Wikipedia: Paraguay (checked 13 Nov 2026); Britannica: history of Paraguay (checked 15 Nov 2026) (independence was declared on 14 May 1811 after the Spanish governor was deposed)
